chapters.title: A Home Behind the Forest
chapters.learningFocus: Identify setting, sequence and the difference between a character’s belief and a fact.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: In 1895, Dracula leaned over his baby daughter, Mavis, and tried to surprise her with a game of peekaboo. She began to cry instead. The powerful vampire quickly became a gentle father, soothing her until she giggled.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: I only meant to make you laugh, little one.

panels.artBrief: Warm nursery, baby Mavis in cot, Dracula’s imposing silhouette bending into an apologetic smile; tender, not frightening.

panels.narration: As Mavis grew, Dracula studied plans for a large hotel. He wanted room for many monster families. To him, the building would be more than a holiday destination: it would be a refuge where his daughter could feel safe.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: We will need plenty of room for our guests.

panels.artBrief: Blueprint spread on table; Dracula points at proposed towers while toddler Mavis crawls along a wall; blueprint is a fictional plan, not a real map.

panels.narration: Mavis was curious about the world beyond their home. During a game with her father, she noticed the way outside and asked about it. Dracula immediately pulled her back and closed the door, ending the game’s cheerful mood.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: We do not go out there.

panels.artBrief: Small Mavis reaches toward a partly open door; father gently pulls her back and shuts it. Keep developmental age consistent within this early-life sequence.

panels.narration: Later, Dracula read her a frightening story about humans chasing monsters. Mavis listened nervously. These were the stories her father chose to tell her; she had not explored the human world and checked those claims for herself.
panels.artBrief: Bedtime book, worried young Mavis and dramatic Dracula. Label the imagined human scene as a story vignette, never as an independently witnessed event.

panels.narration: Dracula reminded Mavis that he had promised her mother he would protect her. His love was clear, but so was his fear. For Mavis, the outside world was becoming a place she knew through warnings rather than experience.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: I promised to keep you safe.

panels.artBrief: Close father-daughter moment; small portrait of Martha in background, without revealing later backstory.

panels.narration: There were happy lessons too. Dracula encouraged Mavis to turn into a bat, bend her legs and push off. She discovered that she could fly. Her father cheered as she practised this surprising new skill.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: Keep going! You are doing it!

panels.artBrief: Young Mavis as one small black bat making a first flight; father encourages her from below. Do not depict a human face attached to an ordinary bat body.

panels.narration: When the hotel was ready, the builder explained its protection. A hidden site, a large haunted forest and a frightening boundary would discourage human visitors. He also gave a warning: bright fires or fireworks could draw unwanted attention.

dialogue.speaker: Builder
dialogue.text: Keep it hidden. No bonfires or fireworks.

panels.artBrief: Builder and Dracula survey the completed castle through thick forest; no invented labelled geography.

panels.narration: Dracula looked at the finished building and thought of Martha. The secret hotel represented a promise to protect their daughter. Yet one question remained beyond its strong walls: would a safe home always be enough for curious Mavis?

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: This is the place we planned for her.

panels.artBrief: Wide reveal of illuminated hotel, Dracula and young Mavis small in foreground; hopeful but slightly enclosed composition.

comprehension.prompt: What warning did the builder give Dracula about bonfires and fireworks?
comprehension.answerGuidance: The builder warned him not to use bonfires or fireworks because they could attract human attention and reveal the hidden hotel.
comprehension.hint: Reread the builder’s warning in panel 7.

comprehension.prompt: Would you describe Dracula’s new hotel as a good solution to his worries? Explain using one detail from the chapter.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a reasoned yes, no or partly: the hidden hotel offers protection, but shutting out the world can limit Mavis. Require a chapter detail; no single preferred opinion.
comprehension.hint: Consider both what the hotel provides and what Mavis still wants to know.

comprehension.prompt: When you are learning a new skill, what kind of encouragement helps you most? Explain why.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a relevant personal or hypothetical example and explanation. The learner need not disclose private experiences or cite the story.
comprehension.hint: Think about helpful words, a demonstration or a chance to practise.

comprehension.prompt: What two actions show that Dracula wants to protect Mavis? Use details from different panels.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Possible evidence: closes the outside door, reassures her about his promise, builds a hidden refuge and checks how humans will be kept away. Distinguish protective intention from whether every decision is wise.
comprehension.hint: Look for both a small action at home and a larger building project.

comprehension.prompt: Why does the author begin with the time label “In 1895”? Explain how it helps you read the later panels.
comprehension.answerGuidance: The date places the opening in the past; later captions show Mavis growing and events moving forward. The label helps the reader follow the time sequence.
comprehension.hint: Compare the first caption with “As Mavis grew” and “Later.”

panels.narration: Hotel Transylvania was ready for visitors. Dracula welcomed monster families and handed out a schedule for Mavis’s birthday celebration. He proudly described the hotel as a place without humans, where his guests could finally relax together.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: Welcome! There is a full celebration planned.

panels.artBrief: Grand lobby bustling with friendly monsters; Dracula gestures toward a printed event schedule. Keep schedule text as editable HTML, not generated lettering.

panels.narration: An urgent plumbing problem interrupted his greeting. A toilet was blocked, and a suit of armour needed the manager’s help. Even in a hotel filled with extraordinary creatures, someone still had to deal with ordinary problems.

dialogue.speaker: Suit of armour
dialogue.text: There is a problem in one of the rooms!

panels.artBrief: Suit of armour carries a discreet plumbing notice; Dracula turns from greeting guests. Bathroom humour remains mild and no mess shown.

panels.narration: Wayne arrived with his lively family. His children raced around, and Dracula reminded them that a hotel was not a place for wild behaviour. The host wanted everyone to enjoy themselves, but he also wanted order.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: Let us keep the lobby under control.

panels.artBrief: Werewolf family with active children and tired parent; clear paths through the lobby and comic motion lines.

panels.narration: Frank arrived in an unusual way: by mail. He explained that he was afraid of flying because an aeroplane might catch fire. His friends knew this worry well and recognised the reason for his strange travel arrangements.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.text: It is the flying that worries me!

panels.narration: Griffin, the Invisible Man, teased Dracula. The host could hear him but could not see a body. Their joking welcome made an ordinary greeting into a guessing game, reminding readers how unusual these old friends were.

chapters.title: The Birthday Promise
chapters.learningFocus: Explain a promise, compare feelings and support an inference with words and pictures.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: Mavis had rehearsed an important conversation. When she turned 118, her father had promised that she could explore beyond the hotel. Now she wanted him to remember that promise, even though she expected him to worry about humans.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: You promised I could go out when I turned 118.

panels.artBrief: Mavis in the established gothic bedroom rehearses toward a closed door; use approved sample visual direction but new editable text.

panels.narration: Dracula arrived with birthday greetings and an invitation to catch scorpions together. Mavis liked spending time with him, but she had something else to discuss. Before she could finish her argument, he gave an answer she had not expected.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: Dad, there is something we need to discuss.

panels.artBrief: Father enters warmly, Mavis raises one finger to speak; two clearly attributed speech bubbles.

panels.narration: Mavis was astonished. She had prepared for a refusal, not permission. Dracula repeated his answer and said she was old enough to make choices. For a moment, all her carefully practised words seemed unnecessary.
panels.artBrief: Close two-shot of Mavis’s surprised face and father’s controlled expression; avoid suggesting he has fully abandoned his fears.

panels.narration: She hugged him and hurried to pack. A postcard had made her curious about Hawaii, which she connected with her parents. The possibility of seeing somewhere new made the world beyond the hotel feel suddenly much larger.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: I want to see the place on this postcard!

panels.artBrief: Open suitcase and postcard with a tropical landscape, no authentic map claim; no embedded unverified caption about parents meeting there.

panels.narration: Dracula was reluctant to let her travel so far. He reminded her that guests had come for her birthday. Mavis replied that she loved them but wanted fresh experiences and a chance to meet someone nearer her own age.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: I love our guests. I also want to see new things.

panels.artBrief: Mavis holds postcard hopefully; Dracula gestures toward hotel festivities outside the bedroom.

panels.narration: Her cautious father suggested a shorter journey: a human village just beyond the cemetery. She could visit and return in about thirty minutes. It was not Hawaii, but Mavis decided that even a small trip would count as exploring.
panels.artBrief: Father proposes a nearby destination without invented map distances; Mavis becomes hopeful.

panels.narration: Mavis thanked him for trusting her. Downstairs, the guests reacted with alarm when they heard her plan. They offered warnings about humans, while Mavis wondered whether people outside might have changed. Their fears did not erase her excitement.
panels.artBrief: Warm hug then small inset of anxious guests; same clothes and time of day, visually distinct sequential moments.

panels.narration: She turned into a bat and flew away. Frank admired Dracula’s apparently calm response, but then noticed that the father had disappeared. Mavis was beginning her adventure; the reader was left wondering why Dracula had quietly slipped away.
panels.artBrief: Mavis as one small bat departing into night; in foreground Frank looks at the empty place where Dracula stood. Keep village reveal for chapter 4.

comprehension.prompt: Where did Dracula say Mavis could go, and approximately how long could she be away?

comprehension.hint: The answer has two parts. Find the shorter journey Dracula suggests.

comprehension.prompt: Would you accept the nearby village as a first trip instead of Hawaii? Explain using something Mavis says or does.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept yes, no or a qualified answer. Relevant support includes her eagerness for any new experience, her larger dream or the birthday visitors. Do not demand agreement with her decision.
comprehension.hint: Think about why a small journey might still matter to her.

comprehension.prompt: How would you prepare to explain an important request to someone? Describe one useful step and why it helps.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a clear preparation strategy and reason. No personal disclosure or story evidence is required.
comprehension.hint: You might plan your reasons, choose a time or practise speaking.

comprehension.prompt: What details suggest that Dracula has not stopped worrying, even after giving permission? Use two panels.
comprehension.answerGuidance: He is reluctant about Hawaii, limits the trip to a nearby village and then disappears. His disappearance raises a question; the learner must not claim this chapter already proves his later plan.
comprehension.hint: Separate what the chapter shows from what you only suspect.

comprehension.prompt: Why is a close-up of Mavis’s face useful in panel 3? Explain how the illustration adds to the narration.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Her widened eyes and surprised expression reinforce “astonished” and the unexpected permission. The image shows her reaction alongside the words.
comprehension.hint: What feeling can you recognise without reading the speech bubble?

chapters.title: A Village Made of Lies
chapters.learningFocus: Review vocabulary and distinguish what a character believes from what the reader knows.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: Mavis flew past the cemetery and reached the village. She was curious about the quiet buildings and looked into a shop window. This was the first place her father had given her permission to explore on her own.
panels.artBrief: Moonlit village street, Mavis landing near shop mannequins; no visitors visible yet.

panels.narration: A figure suddenly appeared with a torch. Another pointed a pitchfork towards her. Their angry cries startled Mavis, who had expected a conversation rather than a threat. She introduced herself and tried to explain that she meant no harm.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: My name is Mavis. I am friendly!

panels.artBrief: Non-graphic threatening silhouettes with props kept at a distance; focus on Mavis’s startled expression.

panels.narration: More villagers gathered and repeated the frightening claims she had heard in her father’s stories. Mavis grew astonished and confused. They talked about biting toes and taking candy instead of listening to her greeting.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: I only wanted to say hello.

panels.artBrief: Crowd of awkwardly posed disguised zombies; costumes slightly odd but reveal not yet explicit to Mavis.

panels.narration: The reader could see something Mavis missed. One supposed human lost a mask, revealing a zombie underneath. Dracula was nearby, directing the scene. He quickly put the disguise back before his daughter understood what had happened.
panels.artBrief: Behind Mavis’s turned back, mask slips off a plainly undead hotel worker; Dracula replaces it. Mild theatrical disguise, no detached anatomy or gore.

panels.narration: The villagers were not ordinary people reacting freely. They were part of a performance designed to frighten her. Dracula wanted to protect Mavis, but he was doing it by controlling what she saw and hiding the truth.
panels.artBrief: Wide staging view reveals Dracula directing disguised staff while Mavis remains isolated in foreground; clearly distinct knowledge positions.

panels.narration: When the clumsy crowd’s torches caused confusion, Mavis still offered help. She did not answer fear with cruelty. However, the noisy encounter convinced her that the world outside the hotel was as dangerous as Dracula had described.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: Are you all right? Can I help?

panels.artBrief: Small harmless-looking stage flame and smoke kept in background; no injury detail. Mavis reaches out to help.

panels.narration: She turned into a bat and hurried home. Her father’s warning now seemed true to her, although the reader knew her evidence had been arranged. Her conclusion came from what she had witnessed, but she had not witnessed the whole truth.
panels.artBrief: Small bat retreats from village toward distant hotel; mood subdued, no new travel route labels.

panels.narration: Dracula watched her leave and believed his plan had worked. He sent the workers back to their duties. The hotel might seem like a refuge again, but the safety he had created depended on a lie his daughter did not know.
panels.artBrief: Costumed staff remove props as Dracula watches departing bat; reveal theatrical town, not a genuine human community.

comprehension.prompt: Who was pretending to be the human villagers?
comprehension.answerGuidance: Zombies from the hotel staff were disguised as humans; Dracula was directing the deception.
comprehension.hint: Look at what the slipping mask reveals.

comprehension.prompt: Do you think Dracula’s wish to protect Mavis excuses his plan? Use a chapter detail to explain your opinion.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a supported view while keeping intention and action distinct. Evidence includes staged threats, hidden disguises and Mavis returning frightened. The task does not require agreement that protection excuses lying.
comprehension.hint: Explain both what he wants and what he actually does.

comprehension.prompt: What could you do before accepting a surprising claim as true? Explain why your step would help.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a sensible check, such as asking for evidence, comparing explanations or consulting a trusted adult. Do not require personal experience.
comprehension.hint: Think about how you could learn whether you have the whole picture.

comprehension.prompt: How is the reader’s understanding of the village different from Mavis’s understanding? Give two details.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Mavis thinks threatening humans prove her father right; the reader sees a zombie’s mask slip and Dracula directing staff. Require both viewpoints and concrete clues.

comprehension.prompt: Why is it useful to show the mask slipping in a separate panel? Explain how the panel sequence changes your understanding.
comprehension.answerGuidance: It reveals the trick before Mavis discovers it and lets the reader compare appearance with reality. Sequencing makes the hidden cause visible.
comprehension.hint: Notice what the reader learns between the greeting and Mavis’s return.

chapters.title: The Comfort of a False Story
chapters.learningFocus: Use dialogue to identify reassurance and distinguish comfort from honesty.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: Dracula slipped back into the hotel. A talking shrunken head noticed his secretive arrival and asked where he had been. He wanted silence rather than questions. The performance outside was over, but he still had to hide his part in it.
panels.artBrief: Comic talking door ornament watches Dracula entering discreetly; stylised toy-like ornament, not realistic remains.

panels.narration: Mavis was already in her room. Her father asked about the world outside as though he did not know what had happened. She answered quietly at first, then admitted that the visit had frightened her.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: You were right about the humans.

panels.artBrief: Subdued bedroom, Mavis sitting on bed and Dracula in doorway acting surprised.

panels.narration: She described the angry villagers and their strange threats. Dracula reacted with concern. He could reassure her that she was safe at home, but he did not tell her that the people who frightened her were his own disguised workers.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: They behaved just as you warned me.

panels.artBrief: Mavis recounts the encounter, with small muted memory inset of the crowd; no new village event.

panels.narration: Mavis now began to doubt her earlier wish to explore. She apologised for questioning her father and said she would never leave again. Dracula had regained her trust, but that trust rested on information he knew was false.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: I am sorry I doubted you. I will stay here.

panels.artBrief: Mavis looks down while father sits nearby; visual contrast between her sadness and his relieved reaction.

panels.narration: Dracula offered wormcakes and promised a wonderful birthday. The familiar food was meant to comfort her. Yet comforting someone and being honest with them are different actions; the chapter shows him doing one while avoiding the other.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: Let me make your birthday special.

panels.artBrief: Tray of whimsical cakes, no realistic worms necessary; warm colours around food but sadness remains visible.

panels.narration: He also reminded her about a present from her mother. Martha had left instructions that it should not be opened until Mavis turned 118. Its contents were still a mystery, giving Mavis something to look forward to.
panels.artBrief: Closed keepsake gift shown without its contents; do not reveal the later book or message prematurely.

panels.narration: Outside the room, the shrunken head questioned him again. Dracula defended his decision, saying he had done what was necessary and that Mavis would thank him one day. His confidence did not make the deception disappear.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: What I thought I had to do.

panels.artBrief: Corridor exchange; father defensive, door ornament doubtful; no new character action beyond source.

panels.narration: Dracula dismissed one of the workers who had helped with the plan. He believed the danger had passed. Behind him, Mavis remained safe inside the hotel, but the adventure she had wanted had been replaced by a fear he had created.
panels.artBrief: Dracula gestures a zombie worker back to work; closed bedroom door forms quiet final image.

comprehension.hint: Think about listening, asking what would help or offering practical support.

comprehension.prompt: How does Dracula behave differently with Mavis and with the shrunken head? Use details from both conversations.
comprehension.answerGuidance: With Mavis he acts concerned, asks about her trip and offers comfort; with the head he seeks silence and defends what he did. The contrast shows what he reveals to each listener.

chapters.title: A Backpack at the Door
chapters.learningFocus: Trace cause and effect and explain why characters interpret the same object differently.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: Dracula’s relief ended when a young traveller appeared inside the hotel. The visitor was Jonathan, a human carrying a backpack. To Dracula, this intruder threatened the rule on which the entire hotel was built.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: Who are you, and how did you find us?

panels.artBrief: Lobby doorway frames friendly red-haired Jonathan with backpack; Dracula freezes in alarm.

panels.narration: Jonathan explained that he had been exploring the mountains. Stories of a spooky forest had interested him. Then he saw unusual figures with flames around them and followed them to the castle, believing he had found something exciting.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: I followed those strange-looking people to this amazing place.

panels.artBrief: Clearly marked flashback of distant workers returning from staged village; flames small and non-graphic; Johnny follows at a distance.

panels.narration: Dracula remembered the builder’s warning about attracting attention. The village performance had helped a human find the hotel. His attempt to keep Mavis away from people had accidentally brought a person straight to her home.
panels.artBrief: Split visual memory: builder’s earlier warning and present anxious Dracula; no duplicate new events.

panels.narration: Jonathan thought the hotel guests were people in costumes. Dracula hurried him away while visitors kept interrupting with questions. He wanted to conceal the newcomer before anyone understood who he really was.
panels.artBrief: Dracula ushers traveller past friendly multi-headed guest asking for help; comic crowd without new named characters.

panels.narration: In a small room, Dracula inspected the backpack as if it might hold dangerous equipment. Ordinary belongings seemed threatening because he expected danger. Jonathan, meanwhile, was confused by the host’s urgent and unfriendly behaviour.
panels.artBrief: Small utility room with travel bag on bench; everyday clothes and headphones, not actual weapons.

panels.narration: Headphones caused another misunderstanding. Dracula imagined that the device might control his mind, while Jonathan explained that it played music. The same object looked harmless to one character and alarming to the other.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: They are headphones. You listen to music.

panels.artBrief: Dracula recoils theatrically from headphones; Jonathan demonstrates calmly. Do not include real song lyrics or commercial music playback.

panels.narration: Dracula worried about more than the guests. If Mavis met a friendly human, she might discover that he had lied about the village. Jonathan still did not understand the danger Dracula imagined or the secret he was protecting.
panels.artBrief: Father glances toward corridor leading to Mavis’s room; Jonathan innocently admires surroundings.

panels.narration: Looking at the supposed costumes gave Dracula an idea. He began changing Jonathan’s appearance so the visitor would look like a monster. A disguise might hide the immediate problem, but it would also create another story to maintain.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: What are you doing to my hair?

panels.artBrief: Makeup tools and costume pieces prepared; reveal of finished disguise reserved for next chapter.

comprehension.prompt: What did Jonathan follow that led him to the castle?
comprehension.answerGuidance: He followed the unusual figures from the staged village, who had flames around them, after exploring the mountains and forest.
comprehension.hint: Focus on the last thing he followed, not only the first story he heard.

comprehension.prompt: Would you have explained the truth to Jonathan or tried to disguise him? Support your choice with a consequence from the chapter.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a supported choice. Truth might reduce misunderstanding; disguise might avoid immediate alarm but creates more concealment. No single opinion is required.
comprehension.hint: Think about immediate trouble and later problems.

comprehension.prompt: How can you find out what an unfamiliar object is before deciding it is dangerous or useless?
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a sensible information-seeking step, such as asking its owner or reading instructions, with a reason. Do not require handling an unsafe object.
comprehension.hint: A careful question can be more useful than a guess.

comprehension.prompt: Explain how Dracula’s village plan helped cause the very problem he wanted to prevent.
comprehension.answerGuidance: The staged village involved conspicuous flames; Jonathan followed the returning figures to the hidden hotel, bringing in a human. Link the earlier action to the present result.
comprehension.hint: Connect the builder’s warning with Jonathan’s explanation.

comprehension.prompt: Why does the author include a brief flashback in panel 2 instead of showing only Jonathan talking in the room?
comprehension.answerGuidance: The flashback makes the route and cause visible, helping the reader understand how he arrived and why Dracula remembers the warning.
comprehension.hint: What earlier event does the picture let you see?

chapters.title: Not Just Costumes
chapters.learningFocus: Recognise an assumption and explain how evidence changes a character’s reaction.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: Jonathan emerged wearing a monster disguise. Dracula hoped to guide him towards the door without attracting attention. Jonathan enjoyed the costume and continued to assume that the surrounding creatures were ordinary people dressed for a party.
panels.artBrief: Jonathan in recognisable Frankenstein-style makeup and clothes, red hair still consistent; Dracula steers him through lobby.

panels.narration: The route was not simple. Quasimodo, the hotel’s chef, approached, and Dracula became occupied with a food complaint. Jonathan’s curiosity pulled him away from the host and towards the other guests.
panels.artBrief: Chef with rat companion and tray of fantasy snacks, no disturbing food close-ups; Johnny drifts toward guests.

panels.narration: Jonathan approached a skeleton guest and reached towards what he believed was a clever costume. The guest objected. This uncomfortable encounter gave him evidence that the bones were real and that he had crossed a personal boundary.
panels.artBrief: Skeleton guest raises a stopping hand as Johnny reaches; depict boundary clearly, no intrusive close-up or sexualised staging.

panels.narration: Suddenly, the room looked different to him. These were real monsters, not actors. Panic replaced his excitement, and he hurried through the crowded hotel. Dracula realised that the visitor was no longer safely beside him.
panels.artBrief: Jonathan startled among benign monster shapes, dynamic but readable motion; no actual attack added.

panels.narration: Jonathan collided with Mavis. They looked at each other and felt an unexpected connection. The busy room seemed to pause for a moment, but Dracula quickly stepped between them before they could talk properly.
panels.artBrief: Gentle eye-contact moment, subtle warm glow; source’s “zing” suggested visually, no sexualised portrayal.

panels.narration: Mavis wanted to know who the newcomer was. Dracula brushed the question aside and hurried Jonathan away. The human was now afraid of the father, while the daughter was becoming interested in the person he was trying to hide.
panels.artBrief: Father blocks line of sight between curious Mavis and shaken traveller; keep emotional acting readable.

panels.narration: In private, Jonathan begged Dracula not to harm him. Dracula explained that he did not drink human blood and used a substitute. Another assumption was being challenged, although the visitor had not yet fully understood the hotel.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: Are you going to hurt me?

panels.artBrief: Private room, non-graphic conversation; no blood shown, substitute explained in narration only.

panels.narration: Jonathan also copied the familiar “bleh, bleh, bleh” voice he associated with Dracula. The count insisted that he did not speak that way. Both characters had entered their meeting with ideas about the other; neither had understood the whole person.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: I do not talk like that!

panels.artBrief: Comic mirrored gestures, Dracula offended and Jonathan sheepish; finish with humour rather than terror.

comprehension.prompt: What did Jonathan first believe about the creatures at the hotel?
comprehension.answerGuidance: He thought they were ordinary people wearing costumes for a party.
comprehension.hint: Find the assumption he makes before meeting the skeleton guest.

comprehension.prompt: Was Dracula’s decision to hide Jonathan likely to make the misunderstandings better or worse? Use one event to explain.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept either or a qualified position with evidence: disguise conceals his identity but leaves him unaware the monsters are real, leading to panic and collision.
comprehension.hint: Consider what Jonathan does not know because nobody explains the situation.

comprehension.prompt: What is a respectful way to ask about something unusual about a person or their belongings? Explain your choice.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept an example of asking politely, seeking permission or not touching without consent, with a reason.
comprehension.hint: Think about permission and personal space.

comprehension.prompt: How do Jonathan’s feelings change from the beginning to the end of the chapter? Use at least two events.
comprehension.answerGuidance: He begins excited about costumes, panics when monsters prove real, then receives information challenging his fear of Dracula. His curiosity or humour partly returns. Require events, not just emotion labels.
comprehension.hint: Track what he learns and how he reacts after each discovery.

comprehension.hint: Compare the two statements and the faces beside them.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: So it is a hotel for monsters?

panels.artBrief: Dracula presents the castle dramatically from window; Johnny sums up with friendly simplicity.

panels.narration: Dracula then turned into a bat and began carrying Jonathan out through the window. He wanted the human gone before Mavis could learn more. The disguise had not solved the problem, so he was trying another route.

panels.narration: He told his daughter that he had invited someone nearer her age to help plan the birthday party. This was not the reason Jonathan had arrived. It was a new explanation invented to conceal the earlier secret.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: He is here to help with your party.

panels.artBrief: Father gestures grandly to improvised planner; Johnny caught between smile and surprise.

panels.narration: Mavis was pleased that her father had sought help. When she said she was 118, Jonathan claimed he was 121. Dracula helped him maintain the story. dialogue.text: Why are you not checking the emergency?

panels.artBrief: Armour waits with urgent posture; Mavis observes father’s hesitation rather than assuming the lie is already exposed.

panels.narration: She offered to keep Jonathan company, but Dracula objected that the visitor needed time to plan. He agreed aloud that they could meet later, then privately told Jonathan the opposite. His public words and private instructions no longer matched.
panels.artBrief: Clearly separated public exchange and private whisper; speech attribution unmistakable.

panels.narration: Dracula led Jonathan away. To Mavis, the stranger appeared to be a young monster helping with her celebration. To the reader, he was a human caught in a growing disguise. Each new explanation protected the secret and complicated it.
panels.artBrief: Father and traveller depart down corridor; Mavis watches with interest, not knowledge of later identity reveal.

chapters.title: The Cousin in the Corridor
chapters.learningFocus: Sequence complications and explain how an invented explanation creates another problem.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: Dracula chose a secret passage to move Jonathan out of the hotel. The tunnels had been designed as an escape route if humans ever invaded. Now the owner was using them to remove one friendly human without his daughter noticing.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: We will leave through the tunnels.

panels.artBrief: Underground corridor, torchlike fantasy lighting without active hazardous flames, father and disguised Jonathan moving quietly.

panels.narration: Unfortunately, knowing that a passage existed was not the same as knowing every door. Dracula opened an occupied room by mistake and apologised. His hurried plan was becoming an awkward tour of places they were not supposed to enter.
panels.artBrief: Door opens only a crack onto surprised fully clothed fantasy guests; no intimate activity shown.

panels.narration: Another door led to another occupied room rather than an exit. Jonathan admired the strange hotel, while Dracula wanted silence so he could think. The visitor saw an adventure; the host saw a growing list of interruptions.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: I need a moment to think.

panels.artBrief: Second closed doorway and “occupied” cue rendered as editable text if used; keep privacy, no bathing or nudity.

panels.narration: The friends interrupted with a problem of their own. They wanted to practise music for Mavis and hoped Dracula would sing with them. He refused, saying he had not sung in public since Martha. The reason carried a sadness the others recognised.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: I am not ready to sing.

panels.artBrief: Bandstand with familiar friends and zombie musicians; Dracula’s expression briefly serious, no invented details of Martha’s death.

panels.narration: Mavis found Jonathan again and asked his name. The simple question made him hesitate. Still wearing his disguise, he called himself Frankenstein, then changed the explanation when she pointed out that her Uncle Frank was nearby.
panels.artBrief: Mavis curious, Jonathan thinking fast, Frank visible near musicians; bubble tail precisely attributed.

panels.narration: Frank approached and said he did not have such a cousin. Dracula joined the conversation to support Jonathan’s claim. Their explanation became more complicated as they tried to make an invented relationship sound believable.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.text: I do not remember a cousin like you.

panels.artBrief: Tall friendly Frank leans forward suspiciously; Dracula moves into gap to help Johnny.

panels.narration: They connected the supposed family relationship to the original owner of Frank’s right arm. It was a wildly unusual explanation, but in this monster hotel it persuaded Frank. Jonathan’s false name now came with an equally false family history.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: On your right-arm side of the family.

panels.artBrief: Frank looks at his own right arm in surprise; playful intact stitched arm, no dismemberment.

panels.narration: Frank welcomed his new “cousin” with an enthusiastic handshake, and Mavis laughed. The escape through the passage had failed. Instead of leaving quietly, Jonathan had become more closely connected to the people Dracula wanted him to avoid.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.text: It is good to meet you!

panels.artBrief: Overenthusiastic handshake lifts Johnny slightly in cartoon exaggeration, happy Mavis and uneasy Dracula.

chapters.title: A Different Kind of Music
chapters.learningFocus: Compare viewpoints and explain how a creative suggestion changes a group’s response.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: The guests wanted to know why Johnnystein had arrived. Dracula repeated the party-planner explanation and said a younger helper could offer a fresh perspective. He had invented the role to hide Jonathan, but the others took it seriously.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: I am helping with the party.

panels.artBrief: Friendly monsters gather around disguised Johnny, Dracula tries to appear relaxed; invisible Griffin represented consistently.

panels.narration: Dracula’s friends wanted to make music for Mavis. They thought the planned entertainment needed more energy. Jonathan invited them to play so he could hear their ideas before suggesting changes.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: Let us hear what you can do!

panels.artBrief: Small band with Frank, Murray, Wayne and invisible drummer; recognisable consistent instruments, avoid impossible extra hands.

panels.narration: Their song remembered Mavis growing up. The affection was genuine, but the rhythm felt old-fashioned to Jonathan. He interrupted the performance and suggested a faster, livelier approach for the birthday celebration.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: Could we make the beat more lively?

panels.artBrief: Band plays gentle familiar tune; younger visitor listens, then raises hand with a suggestion. No film lyrics in artwork.

panels.narration: Dracula briefly thought the interruption meant Jonathan agreed with him. Instead, the human began demonstrating his own idea. A suggestion that sounded useful to the host quickly became another challenge to his carefully controlled plan.
panels.artBrief: Dracula starts approving smile, then looks uneasy as Johnny takes centre stage.

panels.narration: With the band joining in, Jonathan turned the performance into an energetic celebration of Mavis turning 118. The crowd answered him and became involved. The music was no longer something they simply watched from a distance.
panels.artBrief: Bright but gothic bandstand, audience joins call-and-response; exact brief adapted cheer as editable text, no song transcription.

panels.narration: Jonathan attempted a dramatic stage dive and landed on the floor. He treated the mistake as part of the fun rather than the end of it. His enthusiasm mattered more to the guests than a perfectly polished performance.
panels.artBrief: Comic safe landing with exaggerated bounce and no injury, crowd amused and supportive.

panels.narration: Mavis was delighted, and Frank believed his new cousin could make the party wonderful. Other guests suggested more activities. Jonathan’s perspective had given them permission to imagine a celebration different from the usual routine.
panels.artBrief: Mavis bright-eyed among cheering friends, suggestions indicated by gestures rather than cluttered unreadable text.

panels.narration: Dracula refused the new suggestions and insisted on the schedule. The group wanted Jonathan to join them anyway. The disagreement was not only about music: it was about who would decide what fun should look like.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: We are staying with the plan.

panels.narration: The guests moved through the hotel’s activities, including games, exercise and breakfast. Jonathan fitted easily into the group. Dracula watched closely, concerned that ordinary conversation might reveal that the cheerful newcomer was a human.
panels.artBrief: Montage of games and breakfast in four small background vignettes, all from source, foreground Dracula watches Jonathan.

panels.narration: Jonathan talked about places he had visited. Mavis wanted to hear more about the world outside. When she asked about mobs, he understood the word as busy crowds, not the threatening groups she had learned to fear.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: How did you manage the crowds?

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: You learn to go along with things.

panels.artBrief: Breakfast conversation; subtle split thought images of tourist crowd versus feared mob, both clearly character interpretations.

panels.narration: Quasimodo’s rat again sensed a human, making the chef suspicious. Dracula had to improvise. He suddenly ordered many omelettes to distract the kitchen while Jonathan continued talking with the guests.
panels.artBrief: Chef and alert rat at breakfast station; Dracula’s extravagant food order draws attention away, no live cooking hazard detail.

panels.narration: The host privately gave Jonathan a plan. He should pretend to be excited about swimming, then claim that his back hurt and leave. It was another attempt to remove him without explaining the real reason.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: Make an excuse and then go.

panels.artBrief: Private whisper at pool entrance; disguised Johnny nods, public guests not able to hear.

panels.narration: Jonathan’s complaint about his back was misunderstood. Instead of helping him leave, the monsters began climbing onto one another for a pool game. The simple excuse became a chaotic activity that pulled him further into the group.

panels.narration: Mavis joined the game, and everyone became more excited. Dracula tried to stop the rough play. The guests saw harmless fun, but he was watching a particular danger that they did not understand.
panels.artBrief: Happy group splash, Mavis and Johnny participating, Dracula alarmed at water near face makeup.

panels.narration: Water could wash away Jonathan’s makeup and reveal his identity. Dracula warned him, but the visitor prepared another jump. The disguise depended on a thin layer that the pool could easily remove.
panels.artBrief: Close-up of small makeup streak on Johnny’s cheek contrasted with pool, identity not fully exposed yet.

panels.narration: Dracula used magic to stop Jonathan in midair and arrange a soft landing on Blobby. The guests saw an unusual rescue. The reader knew he was also preventing the disguise from failing, so the same action served two purposes.

chapters.title: A Sunrise from the Shadows
chapters.learningFocus: Review vocabulary and compare inherited fears with a different account of experience.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: Dracula took Jonathan away from the pool and scolded him. The visitor believed the guests were finally having fun. The host believed the activity was out of control. Their disagreement revealed two different perspectives on the same events.
panels.artBrief: Cemetery-side confrontation in shade or nighttime before dawn; father stern, Johnny frustrated, no new physical threat.

panels.narration: Dracula tried to use his powers to erase Jonathan’s memory of the hotel. It did not work. Jonathan suggested that his contact lenses might be interfering, which was his explanation rather than something the story independently proved.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: Perhaps it is my contact lenses.

panels.artBrief: Fantasy hypnotic eyes contrasted with ordinary contact-lens explanation; no eye-touching demonstration.

panels.narration: The count finally ordered him to leave and never return. Jonathan walked away, unhappy about the experiences he would miss. The threat made him hesitate when a bat appeared nearby, until he realised it was Mavis rather than her father.
panels.artBrief: Disappointed Johnny on path, small bat approaches and becomes Mavis in clear sequential motion; no second unidentified bat.

panels.narration: Mavis invited him to a high viewpoint. He initially said he had to go, but her promise of an interesting experience changed his mind. Soon they were looking out together from the hotel roof.
panels.artBrief: Safe fictional rooftop viewing area, stone ledge and broad landscape; no instruction for real-world climbing.

panels.narration: They talked about travel and Hawaii. Mavis asked whether humans had treated Jonathan in the frightening ways her father described. He answered with an ordinary story about someone taking too much of his snack, not a tale of monsters being hunted.
panels.artBrief: Quiet two-shot; tiny memory vignette of a shared snack, clearly Jonathan’s recollection, no invented major travel event.

panels.narration: Their conversation began to reveal a different picture of people. Jonathan valued exploring rather than staying in one place. Mavis listened to a perspective based on travel, although she still did not know he was human.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: There is so much to discover.

panels.artBrief: Mavis listening thoughtfully, wide horizon outside castle, tension between open view and sheltered position.

panels.narration: As the sun rose, light reached Mavis and she immediately moved back. Sunlight was dangerous to her in this fantasy story. Jonathan noticed the problem and realised that she had rarely been able to watch a sunrise.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: I need to stay in the shade.

panels.artBrief: Thin edge of sunlight on roof, Mavis retreats into shadow; no visible burns or distress close-up.

panels.narration: Jonathan found a way for her to watch while remaining in shadow. The new view did not require her to ignore a real limit; it required someone to consider that limit. Together they watched the morning colours spread across the sky.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: Stay here in the shade and look.

panels.artBrief: Beautiful sunrise seen from deep architectural shade, Mavis fully protected, Johnny beside her; no direct sunlight on her skin.

chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: While Mavis and Jonathan watched the morning outside, Dracula rested with his friends in the hotel’s sauna. The others talked warmly about the visitor. They enjoyed his company and had noticed how happily Mavis laughed with him.

dialogue.speaker: Wayne
dialogue.text: That young visitor is fun to be around.

panels.artBrief: Comfortably seated friends in steamy spa room wearing modest robes or coverings; no body-focused framing.

panels.narration: Dracula resisted the idea that Mavis and Jonathan might grow close. He said she could not be with someone of Jonathan’s kind. His friends, who believed the visitor was Frank’s cousin, understood the comment differently from the reader.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.text: What is wrong with someone like us?

panels.artBrief: Frank looks hurt, Dracula caught off guard; visual thought cues distinguish reader knowledge without exposing the secret to friends.

panels.narration: The awkward conversation forced Dracula to search for another explanation. He claimed to mean Jonathan’s red, curly hair. Griffin objected because, although nobody could see it, he said he had red, curly hair too.
panels.artBrief: Invisible Griffin represented by spectacles and robe; never render his head as visible. Dracula cannot see the hair.

panels.narration: Above them, Mavis was still admiring the sunrise that Jonathan had helped her see. The reader could compare her actual happiness with the worried discussion below. Her experience was not the same as the future Dracula imagined for her.
panels.artBrief: Return to protected rooftop shade from chapter12; clear location transition caption or panel background, no sun exposure.

panels.narration: Back in the sauna, Dracula made a new claim: Jonathan had left because he disliked Mavis and the guests. The friends were surprised. They could not see the rooftop, so they had little evidence with which to challenge him.
panels.artBrief: Father asserts story while friends react with disappointment; keep claim in speech, not narrator’s factual voice.

panels.narration: At that moment, Jonathan stepped onto a weak part of the roof and fell through. The interruption was sudden and unplanned. No careful explanation could prepare Dracula for the visitor arriving directly in the middle of his story.
panels.artBrief: Cartoon roof panel gives way, small plaster pieces, safe fantasy fall; no injury detail or depiction as a real-life stunt.

panels.narration: Jonathan landed on Dracula, creating an unmistakable contradiction. The person who had supposedly gone was right there. Dracula stared at him angrily while Jonathan gave a nervous greeting, trapped between the truth and the invented explanation.
panels.artBrief: Comic landing on seated Dracula, both uninjured; friends stare in surprise, simple clear composition.

panels.narration: Frank suggested that Jonathan must have changed his mind. The visitor’s return delighted the friends but exposed another weakness in Dracula’s story. The reader could see how difficult it was becoming to keep every claim consistent with events.
panels.artBrief: Frank amused, others relieved, Dracula exasperated; finish comic misunderstanding without a full identity revelation.

comprehension.prompt: What reason did Dracula give for Jonathan supposedly leaving?
comprehension.answerGuidance: He claimed Jonathan did not like Mavis or the other guests. Make clear that this was Dracula’s claim, not a verified reason.
comprehension.hint: Look for the explanation Dracula gives before the interruption.

comprehension.prompt: Would Jonathan’s sudden return make you question Dracula’s explanation? Support your view with evidence.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a reasoned response; appearing immediately contradicts the implication that he is gone, although friends could imagine he changed his mind. Require evidence and acknowledge uncertainty where relevant.
comprehension.hint: Consider both the claim and what happens next.

comprehension.prompt: What is a polite question you could ask when someone’s explanation does not match what you observe?
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a clear, non-accusatory request for clarification with a reason. No personal example is necessary.
comprehension.hint: Try asking how the two pieces of information fit together.

comprehension.prompt: Compare what the friends believe, what Dracula claims and what the reader knows about Jonathan.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Friends believe he is a welcome monster visitor and later may have changed his mind; Dracula claims he left because he dislikes them; the reader sees him on the roof with Mavis before the fall. Require these distinct viewpoints.
comprehension.hint: Use the rooftop panel as well as the sauna conversation.

comprehension.prompt: Why does the page switch between the rooftop and the sauna? Explain how this layout helps the reader understand the joke.
comprehension.answerGuidance: The switch supplies information the people below do not have, setting up the contradiction when Jonathan falls through. The reader knows the claim is wrong before the characters see him.
comprehension.hint: What do you know just before Dracula makes his claim?

chapters.title: The Flying-Table Race
chapters.learningFocus: Explain how shared play changes a relationship without erasing earlier disagreements.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: Dracula was angry that Jonathan had remained in the hotel. He gave the visitor a tiring job: moving tables into position for the party. Jonathan objected that being trapped there helped him understand how Mavis might feel.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: Now I understand why she wants to leave.

panels.artBrief: Large ballroom with numbered tables, Dracula points to work area; Johnny in established disguise, visibly frustrated.

panels.narration: When Jonathan dragged a table across the floor, the scraping noise annoyed Dracula. The host sent him to a corner and used magic to arrange the furniture himself. Each table moved when he called out its number and destination.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: Table fifty-seven, move to position twenty-three.

panels.artBrief: Magic table movement with editable number badges; no requirement to reproduce all source table numbers or imply arithmetic lesson.

panels.narration: Jonathan watched in amazement. The floating tables suggested a game rather than a chore. He began calling instructions too, turning an orderly arrangement into a moving course that was far more exciting than pushing furniture.
panels.artBrief: Johnny notices airborne tables and leans forward with growing excitement, clear staging before riding.

panels.narration: Soon he was riding the tables and challenging Dracula. Competition replaced the argument. The host responded with commands of his own, trying to block the visitor’s route while keeping up with his playful moves.
panels.artBrief: Dynamic but clearly magical table race inside ballroom; fictional impossible physics, no real stunt instructions.

panels.narration: Their laughter made the change in mood obvious. Dracula was no longer merely supervising a troublesome guest. For a few moments, both characters enjoyed the same game and responded to each other’s ideas.
panels.artBrief: Wide expressive action frame, Dracula grins while Johnny banks on a floating tabletop; motion lines, coherent hands and feet.

panels.narration: They had to react to the same moving space, even while trying to win. The play gave them a chance to cooperate in creating fun rather than argue about its definition. Their delight was something they could share directly.
panels.artBrief: Race reaches playful near-tie; show shared smile and clear separate table positions, not collision.

panels.narration: Meanwhile, Quasimodo was still searching for the human. His suspicion had not disappeared while the others were playing. When Dracula finally stopped laughing and looked for Jonathan, the visitor was no longer beside him.
panels.artBrief: Chef and rat lurking at doorway in background, then empty space beside Dracula; do not show capture details beyond next chapter.

panels.narration: Dracula admitted that the race had been fun, then recognised a possible problem. He called for Quasimodo and hurried after the missing visitor. The shared game had changed his feelings, but the secret still placed Jonathan at risk.
panels.artBrief: Joy shifts to concern in father’s face, numbered tables settle behind him, doorway leads into next chapter.

comprehension.prompt: How did Dracula move the tables without pushing them?
comprehension.answerGuidance: He used magic and called out the tables’ numbers and the positions where they should move.
comprehension.hint: Identify both the power and the commands he uses.

comprehension.prompt: Do you think the race is an important turning point in Dracula and Jonathan’s relationship? Use a detail to explain.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a supported judgement: they laugh, respond to each other’s ideas and share enjoyment, though the secret and conflict are not fully resolved.
comprehension.hint: A turning point can be a change in direction rather than a complete solution.

comprehension.prompt: How can a friendly competition stay enjoyable for everyone? Explain one useful rule or behaviour.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept fairness, respect, adapting rules or noticing discomfort with a reason.
comprehension.hint: Think about how competitors treat each other, not only who wins.

comprehension.prompt: How does Dracula’s attitude change from panel 1 to panel 8? Support your answer with two specific moments.
comprehension.answerGuidance: He starts angry and assigns work; then laughs and joins the game; finally admits enjoyment and becomes concerned when Jonathan is missing. Require at least two stages with evidence.
comprehension.hint: Track his actions as well as the expression on his face.

comprehension.prompt: How do the numbered table labels and action pictures help readers follow the race?
comprehension.answerGuidance: Numbers link Dracula’s commands to particular tables; visual positions and motion show movement that the dialogue alone would not make clear. Do not require decoding every table number.
comprehension.hint: What helps you connect a command with a moving object?

chapters.title: The Kitchen Rescue
chapters.learningFocus: Connect simultaneous events and evaluate a character through an important choice.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: As Dracula searched for Jonathan, Mavis asked where the visitor had gone. Her interest was difficult to hide. Dracula questioned her feelings, while she tried to sound less impressed than she really was.
panels.artBrief: Corridor conversation, daughter trying to appear casual, father distracted by search.

panels.narration: Mavis pointed out that she could not remain at the hotel forever. She wanted to make choices about her own future. Dracula still saw her as very young, even though the chapter made clear that they understood growing up differently.
panels.artBrief: Father-daughter exchange near shaded window, open world beyond but Mavis safely indoors.

panels.narration: Messages from the hotel staff interrupted them. Quasimodo was taking Jonathan towards the kitchen. Dracula ordered the staff to intercept the chef before he reached it, but the attempts to stop him failed.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: Stop him before he reaches the kitchen!

panels.artBrief: Suit of armour receives urgent order; chef moves past guards in comic action without violence detail.

panels.narration: Dracula left Mavis and hurried after them. The reader could now see a change from his earlier attempts to send Jonathan away. He was preparing a rescue rather than treating the visitor only as a problem to remove.
panels.artBrief: Dracula strides down corridor with determined expression; background Mavis left puzzled, no new conversation invented.

panels.narration: In the kitchen, Quasimodo accused Jonathan of being human. Dracula insisted that he was a member of Frank’s family. The disguise was still their explanation, but the chef wanted a demonstration rather than another claim.

dialogue.speaker: Quasimodo
dialogue.text: Then prove he is a monster.

panels.artBrief: Whimsical kitchen, Johnny held at a safe distance from appliances, rat on counter; no cooking-a-person imagery.

panels.narration: Quasimodo told Jonathan to frighten his rat. Jonathan tried several monster noises, but the attempt did not convince the chef. The test threatened to reveal the secret that Dracula had worked so hard to conceal.
panels.artBrief: Johnny tries comically weak scary face; rat unimpressed, chef suspicious; expressive rather than genuinely frightening.

panels.narration: When Quasimodo began announcing that a human was in the hotel, Dracula used magic to freeze him. The chef could no longer speak clearly. The immediate danger was stopped, although the truth itself had not changed.
panels.artBrief: Chef frozen in a harmless magical pose, no ice injury; clear interruption of speech, rat beside him.

panels.narration: Jonathan expressed gratitude for the rescue. Dracula did not simply order him out again. Instead, he said there was something he needed to show him, opening the possibility of a more honest conversation between them.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: There is something you should see.

panels.artBrief: Quiet exit from kitchen, two characters side by side instead of captor and captive; warm transition.

comprehension.prompt: What did Quasimodo ask Jonathan to do to prove he was a monster?
comprehension.answerGuidance: He asked Jonathan to frighten his rat.
comprehension.hint: Find the test rather than the accusation.

comprehension.prompt: Does Dracula’s rescue suggest that his feelings about Jonathan are changing? Explain with a chapter detail.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a supported view: he orders an interception, rushes to help and stops the chef. The rescue may protect the secret as well as the visitor; allow both motives.
comprehension.hint: Consider whether one action can have more than one reason.

comprehension.prompt: How can you show gratitude when someone helps you solve a difficult problem? Explain why your response would matter.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a specific thanks or helpful action and a reason. Do not require a real private incident.
comprehension.hint: Think beyond saying a single word: what could you acknowledge?

comprehension.prompt: What steps does Dracula take before and during the rescue? Put at least three in order.
comprehension.answerGuidance: He orders staff to intercept Quasimodo, leaves to follow when that fails, defends the disguise in the kitchen, then freezes the chef. Require at least three in correct order.
comprehension.hint: Follow the movement from corridor to kitchen.

comprehension.prompt: Why do the narration boxes explain what is happening elsewhere while Mavis speaks with Dracula?
comprehension.answerGuidance: They connect simultaneous concerns: the father-daughter discussion and Jonathan’s danger. The reader understands why Dracula is distracted and leaves suddenly.
comprehension.hint: What important event would be missing if we heard only Mavis’s dialogue?

chapters.title: The Story Behind the Portrait
chapters.learningFocus: Review vocabulary; distinguish a legend, a witness’s account and an unresolved prediction.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: Dracula brought Jonathan to his room and showed him a portrait. Jonathan recognised the woman from a picture he had seen at the ruins of Castle Lubov. He had heard a legend about her and the count who loved her.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: I have seen her picture before.

panels.artBrief: Private room with respectful portrait of Martha; Jonathan recognises image, Dracula solemn.

panels.narration: Jonathan retold the story he knew. A count and a woman had fallen in love, made a home and had a child. According to the legend, a mysterious fire had killed both parents. It was a moving story, but not a complete account.
panels.artBrief: Story-within-story illustrated in framed memory panels; distinguish reported legend with a visual border and caption.

panels.narration: Dracula corrected an important claim: only the wife had died. He explained that humans had attacked their home and that Martha was killed in the fire. This was his account of a loss he had personally experienced, not a rumour Jonathan had collected.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: The legend did not tell the whole truth.

panels.artBrief: Solemn face and distant symbolic burning-castle silhouette; no attack detail, bodies or gore. Grief treated gently.

panels.narration: He had built the hotel to protect their daughter. Knowing this history helped Jonathan understand the fear behind the rules. It explained Dracula’s choices without automatically making every lie or restriction fair.
panels.artBrief: Dracula with small memory of baby Mavis in his arms, then present hotel; visually distinguish past and present.

panels.narration: Dracula acknowledged that Jonathan was a good person. However, he still feared what might happen if monsters trusted the human world. His experience with one visitor had begun to change his view, but it had not removed years of worry.
panels.artBrief: Father addresses visitor directly, posture softens; shared-table composition rather than confrontational blocking.

panels.narration: Jonathan argued that people could be different now. Dracula asked whether he could guarantee that everyone would accept monsters. Jonathan could not promise that. Their discussion ended with uncertainty, not proof that all humans were either kind or cruel.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: I cannot promise what everyone will do.

panels.artBrief: Quiet honest exchange, no crowds used to imply universal evidence; close expressive faces.

panels.narration: Jonathan offered to leave so that Mavis and Dracula would not be hurt. Dracula instead asked him to stay through the birthday party before going. Gratitude for the rescue and sympathy for the father had changed the tone of their conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: Stay until the party is over.

panels.artBrief: Reluctant agreement, party decorations visible through doorway but celebration has not yet begun.

panels.narration: They ended with an imitation of Dracula’s powers and a joke about Wayne. Their shared delight did not solve the disagreement, but it showed a real connection beneath it. For the first time, a difficult truth had brought them closer than a disguise.
panels.artBrief: Gentle humorous imitation, Dracula briefly howls like a werewolf as in source; no new promise of permanent acceptance.

comprehension.prompt: Does learning Dracula’s history change how you understand his behaviour? Explain without assuming that understanding means agreeing.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a supported response: grief explains his fear and protective goal, but learners may still object to deception or restrictions. Keep explanation separate from justification.

comprehension.prompt: What should you say when someone asks you to promise an outcome that you cannot control?
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept honest limits, a narrower promise about one’s own actions or explaining uncertainty, with a reason.
comprehension.hint: Think about what you can genuinely promise.

comprehension.prompt: How does Jonathan’s response change as he learns more? Use two moments from the chapter.
comprehension.answerGuidance: He begins by confidently retelling a legend; listens to the correction, recognises Dracula’s loss, acknowledges limits to guarantees and offers to leave. Require two supported changes.
comprehension.hint: Compare his first story with his later offer.

comprehension.prompt: Why should the legend and Dracula’s memory be shown with different visual framing?
comprehension.answerGuidance: Different borders or captions help readers distinguish a second-hand story from his personal account and avoid treating both versions as equally confirmed within the narrative.
comprehension.hint: What would become confusing if both versions looked like one uninterrupted factual scene?

chapters.title: A Party with a Breaking Point
chapters.learningFocus: Trace how a disagreement develops and distinguish a character’s wish from another character’s response.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: The birthday celebration began with music, decorations and excited guests. Dracula’s plans and Jonathan’s additions had come together. For a while, the party seemed to give everyone a reason to forget the earlier arguments.
panels.artBrief: Lavish gothic ballroom, warm jewel colours, familiar cast dancing; no new named guests or unexplained visual changes.

panels.narration: Mavis thanked Jonathan for making the event special. He asked whether she liked the small changes he had made. Their conversation was warm and easy, unlike the tense explanations that had brought him into the hotel.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: Do you like the new touches?

panels.artBrief: Two young adults speaking beside dance floor, lively celebration behind, facial expressions legible.

panels.narration: Mavis moved closer and kissed Jonathan. He had seemed nervous, but she was ready to show her feelings. The moment was brief and affectionate; it also brought the conflict her father feared into the centre of the celebration.
panels.artBrief: Brief age-appropriate affectionate kiss or just-before/after moment, no sexualisation; both portrayed as established adult fantasy characters.

panels.narration: Dracula rushed to interrupt them. He was upset after the private conversation he had shared with Jonathan. Mavis did not know everything the two had discussed, so her father’s reaction felt like another attempt to control her choices.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: Dad, it was only a kiss.

panels.artBrief: Father steps between them, upset but not physically violent; Johnny startled, Mavis firm.

panels.narration: Mavis reminded him that she was allowed to like someone and wanted to see the world. Their argument raised a question about a boundary: when does caring guidance become an attempt to decide another person’s entire future?

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: I need to make choices too.

panels.artBrief: Mavis stands upright at respectful distance from father, guests begin noticing argument.

panels.narration: She suggested visiting the village again. Perhaps she could show the people that monsters could be friendly. Dracula rejected the idea at once. Mavis kept asking how he could be certain that another visit would make no difference.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: How can you be so sure?

panels.artBrief: Mavis hopeful but challenging, father increasingly cornered; no new village imagery that implies genuine town.

panels.narration: Each answer led to another question. Dracula could not explain his certainty honestly without exposing the plan he had hidden. The music and celebration continued around a conversation that was becoming impossible to contain.
panels.artBrief: Tight close-ups interspersed with party context; tension expressed through posture and speech, not aggression.

panels.narration: Finally, he shouted that the village did not really exist. The music stopped. Guests stared, and Mavis was left with a shocking new question: if the place was not real, what exactly had her father made her believe?
panels.artBrief: Wide frozen ballroom tableau, musicians stop mid-action, Mavis stunned; end on confession without next chapter’s explanation.

comprehension.hint: Look for the revelation at the end, not the earlier disagreement.

comprehension.prompt: Was Mavis reasonable to keep asking how Dracula knew another visit would fail? Use the conversation to support your opinion.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a supported answer: she asks for the reason behind his certainty and proposes trying friendship; learners may discuss the timing or tone without denying her question.
comprehension.hint: What explanation has he given, and what has he avoided explaining?

comprehension.prompt: How can someone disagree with a rule while keeping a conversation respectful? Give one specific approach and explain it.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept asking for the reason, describing a concern, proposing an alternative or choosing a calmer time, with an explanation.
comprehension.hint: Focus on a practical way to express disagreement.

comprehension.prompt: How does the mood change across the chapter? Use one detail from the beginning, middle and ending.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Beginning: joyful party and thanks; middle: interrupted affection and escalating argument; ending: music stops after the confession. Require evidence for all three stages.
comprehension.hint: Track the guests and music as well as the main characters.

comprehension.prompt: Why is the final revelation shown in a wide panel with the whole room reacting?
comprehension.answerGuidance: It shows that the secret is now public and that the event affects more than the two speakers. The silent or stopped performance contrasts with the opening celebration.
comprehension.hint: How would a close-up of Dracula alone give you less information?

chapters.title: When the Disguises Fall
chapters.learningFocus: Analyse two revelations and use present evidence without assuming hidden motives are fully known.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: Mavis demanded an explanation. Dracula admitted that he had built the village and dressed hotel workers as its people. The frightening visit had been a deception planned by the person she trusted most.
panels.artBrief: Father admits truth before crowd; inset of staged village clearly labelled as explanation of previous events, not new event.

panels.narration: He said he could not bear the thought of something happening to her. Mavis answered that lying and keeping her inside forever hurt her too. Their disagreement now concerned trust, not simply whether a journey was safe.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: You knew how much I wanted to explore.

panels.artBrief: Daughter hurt and firm, father pleading; physical distance grows, no melodramatic injury imagery.

panels.narration: Before they could resolve the argument, Quasimodo appeared. He was still unable to speak normally after Dracula’s magic. A fly translated his muffled accusation: a human had been brought into the hotel.

dialogue.speaker: Fly
dialogue.text: He says there is a human here.

panels.artBrief: Frozen-posture chef with speaking fly beside him; audience reacts, speech tails clearly distinguish translation from original sounds.

panels.narration: The guests struggled to believe the claim. Frank insisted that Jonathan was his cousin. Then the rat scrambled over Jonathan and rubbed away his makeup. The disguise failed, exposing an identity that the crowd had never expected.
panels.artBrief: Makeup wipes away visibly without aggression or scratching; original red-haired human Johnny emerges, guests surprised.

panels.narration: Mavis asked Jonathan directly whether he was human. He admitted it and apologised. She moved closer instead of running away, making clear that this discovery did not erase her feelings for him.
panels.artBrief: Close conversation amid blurred alarmed crowd, Mavis extends a supportive hand or embraces him.

panels.narration: For a moment, Jonathan seemed ready to return her affection. Then he looked at Dracula and remembered their earlier conversation. The reader could see hesitation, but Mavis had not heard that private discussion and could not know everything behind it.
panels.artBrief: Johnny’s glance shifts from Mavis to anxious Dracula; small neutral flashback cue to their earlier room, no unseen new command.

panels.narration: Jonathan then said he did not want to be with her because she was a monster. The words were cruel and different from the connection they had shared. He left, giving Mavis no clear explanation for this sudden rejection.
panels.artBrief: Johnny turns toward exit, conflicted face, Mavis deeply hurt; narration carries source’s cruel statement without sensationalised dialogue.

panels.narration: Mavis blamed her father and flew away. Other guests also began to leave, angry and frightened by the secrets. Dracula’s effort to prevent pain had helped create a room full of it, and the celebration had fallen apart.
panels.artBrief: Small bat exits high doorway, guests moving toward lobby, Dracula alone in centre of once-busy ballroom.

comprehension.prompt: How was Jonathan’s human identity revealed to the guests?
comprehension.answerGuidance: Quasimodo accused him through a translator, and the rat removed his makeup so the disguise failed. The physical reveal is the key required detail.

comprehension.prompt: Do you agree with Mavis that Jonathan being human should not erase their friendship or feelings? Use a detail from this chapter or a named earlier chapter.

comprehension.hint: Consider what a person does as well as the group they belong to.

comprehension.prompt: How can someone say no or explain a difficult decision without being deliberately hurtful?
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept honest, respectful wording and a reason. No need for a personal experience.
comprehension.hint: Think about explaining a decision without insulting the other person.

comprehension.prompt: What two deceptions are exposed, and how does each affect Mavis?
comprehension.answerGuidance: The village was staged by her father, damaging trust; Jonathan was disguised as a monster, but Mavis initially accepts his humanity. His later rejection then hurts her. Keep discovery and rejection distinct.
comprehension.hint: Does she react the same way to both revelations?
