chapters.title: The Gift and the Silence
chapters.learningFocus: Explain a symbolic object and distinguish a character’s painful conclusion from an objective fact.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: The hotel was no longer full of birthday excitement. Guests complained and prepared to go. Dracula searched for Mavis, calling her name through the quiet left behind by the broken celebration.
panels.artBrief: After-party corridor with abandoned decorations, father searching; avoid implying every guest has already left.

panels.narration: When he found her, Mavis asked him to erase her memories. Dracula refused. Although he had earlier tried that power on Jonathan, he now said there was too much he wanted his daughter to remember.
panels.artBrief: Private room, respectful emotional distance, no visual depiction of memory erasure or self-harm.

panels.narration: Mavis concluded that humans hated monsters. Jonathan’s rejection seemed to confirm what her father had always said. The reader should recognise this as her painful conclusion, not proof about every human being.
panels.artBrief: Mavis looks away, Johnny’s departure as muted memory inset; caption signals viewpoint rather than universal claim.

panels.narration: Dracula began talking about other monsters she might meet, but then noticed what she was reading. The present Martha had left was now open. The keepsake carried words from the mother whose absence shaped both their lives.
panels.artBrief: Open illustrated keepsake in Mavis’s hands; readable passage is separate editable text, not tiny baked lettering.

panels.narration: Martha’s message described the connection she and Dracula had felt and hoped that Mavis would find love too. It asked her to cherish that connection when it came. The message held hope, even though Mavis was struggling to feel any.
panels.artBrief: Warm small illustrated memory of two bats meeting within book, clearly storybook page; not a new live Martha scene.

panels.narration: Mavis said she had believed she and Jonathan shared that special connection. Now she thought it had mattered only to her. Her despair came from the difference between what she had hoped and what he had said when he left.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: I thought we felt the same thing.

panels.artBrief: Close-up of Mavis’s face beside open gift, restrained tears, compassionate tone.

panels.narration: She told Dracula that she no longer had a reason to leave or dreams to follow. Staying at the hotel was no longer a happy choice; it was the result of feeling defeated. This was not the safe future her father had imagined.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: I do not have any dreams left.

panels.artBrief: Wide room framing makes once-cosy bedroom seem enclosed, father recognises effect; no hopeless message endorsed by narrator.

panels.narration: Dracula finally faced the effect of his actions. His regret was not about losing control of the party but about hurting his daughter. Thinking of Martha, he asked himself what he had done, leaving the reader waiting for a different kind of decision.
panels.artBrief: Father alone beside doorway, daughter and keepsake visible deeper in room; quiet reflective closing frame.

comprehension.hint: What could you say without dismissing the character’s feelings?

comprehension.prompt: Why does Mavis’s decision to stay at the hotel not mean Dracula’s plan has succeeded? Use two details.

comprehension.hint: Compare physical safety with how she feels about her future.

comprehension.prompt: How does the illustration of the open keepsake help connect the past with the present?
comprehension.answerGuidance: It brings Martha’s earlier hopes into Mavis’s current disappointment and reminds readers why the gift matters to both father and daughter. The book is an object linking times.
comprehension.hint: What earlier person and hope enter the scene through this object?

chapters.title: A Search That Begins with Sorry
chapters.learningFocus: Review vocabulary and evaluate an apology through the actions that follow it.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: Dracula stopped the departing guests and asked them to help find Jonathan. They were angry about the deception and frightened of humans. Before they would listen, he had to acknowledge that the story he had told them was wrong.
panels.artBrief: Busy checkout lobby, suitcases and frustrated guests; father stands without his former commanding pose.

panels.narration: He admitted that he had lied. He also said he no longer knew whether his old judgement of humans was right. This was different from replacing one absolute claim with another: he was beginning to admit what he did not know.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: I was wrong about what I told you.

panels.artBrief: Honest direct address, guests listening cautiously, no instant universal approval.

panels.narration: Frank remembered that he had liked Jonathan regardless of the cousin story. Dracula explained that Mavis and Jonathan had felt a special connection and that he had interfered. His regret now included naming the choice he needed to repair.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.text: I liked him, cousin or not.

panels.artBrief: Frank steps forward, other friends reconsider; emphasise remembered behaviour over label.

panels.narration: The friends agreed to help. Even the problem of daylight would not stop Dracula from trying. He did not yet have every answer, but he was willing to leave the place he had built to avoid uncertainty.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: We will have to find a way.

panels.artBrief: Core search party at hotel exit, sunlight outside and shade within; establish protective travel arrangements without new mechanics.

panels.narration: They began by following Jonathan’s boot prints. When the trail became less useful, a piece of clothing from his backpack provided another clue. Dracula hoped Wayne’s sense of smell would help them continue the search.
panels.artBrief: Close-ups of boot prints and dropped shirt, clear detective-style visual evidence, no invented forensic measurements.

panels.narration: Wayne explained that his old tracking ability was not reliable after years of family life. He called on his children instead. Most were distracted, but Winnie stepped forward and carefully examined the scent on the clothing.
panels.artBrief: Small werewolf child Winnie attentive among energetic siblings; keep age and proportions childlike, no dangerous solo task.

panels.narration: In an exaggerated fantasy feat, Winnie identified a car journey and Jonathan’s airport flight. She said it would leave at eight o’clock, and Dracula realised they had about fifteen minutes. The useful clue turned a vague search into an urgent destination.
panels.artBrief: Winnie gives report, Dracula alarmed; editable fictional clue card may show “8:00” and “about 15 minutes”; not real travel information.

panels.narration: The friends hurried towards the airport and overcame a blocked road together. Dracula’s regret had become action. To cherish Mavis’s hopes now meant doing something he had once resisted: entering the outside world and asking others for help.
panels.artBrief: Search group in vehicle moving past road obstruction, no depiction of sheep being eaten; forward motion towards daylight city.

comprehension.prompt: What is one action that could help repair a mistake after an apology? Explain why it would matter.

comprehension.hint: Choose an action connected to the harm, not just a reward or gift.

comprehension.prompt: How does the group combine different contributions to make progress? Give three details.

comprehension.prompt: Why are the boot prints and clothing shown in close-up panels?

chapters.title: The People Holding the Capes
chapters.learningFocus: Revise a judgement using evidence while avoiding a new unsupported generalisation.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: The search party entered a town full of people dressed as monsters. A festival blocked the road to the airport. Dracula and his friends had expected danger, but the first surprise was that humans were celebrating creatures like them.
panels.artBrief: Lively human monster-costume festival, friendly crowd, no unrelated real town landmarks or real brands.

panels.narration: Dracula asked someone dressed as a vampire for directions. The route was crowded, and the answer did not solve the time problem. His friends suggested continuing on foot, while sunlight made every delay more difficult for him.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: How do we reach the airport?

panels.artBrief: Real Dracula and costumed festivalgoer mirror outfits, humorous mistaken identity; shade maintained initially.

panels.narration: The group considered revealing who they really were. Their old prejudice had made them expect every human to be an enemy. Now the festival offered evidence that their picture of people had been incomplete, even if one crowd could not represent everyone.
panels.artBrief: Search party confers under cover, crowd joyful behind; reflective narration, no universal claim of human goodness.

panels.narration: Frank tried to frighten the crowd into recognising him. Instead of running away, people cheered and asked for his attention. The response challenged the fear on which the hotel’s isolation had been based.

dialogue.speaker: Festivalgoer
dialogue.text: We know who you are! We love you!

panels.artBrief: Frank’s theatrical roar met with cheers and autograph request; no aggression or injury.

panels.narration: He explained that Dracula needed to reach the airport for his daughter. The crowd listened to a problem rather than judging only an unfamiliar appearance. A possible confrontation became an opportunity for cooperation.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.text: He needs your help to reach the airport.

panels.artBrief: Frank addressing crowd, Dracula shaded nearby; humans attentive, clear spatial geography.

panels.narration: Someone asked why Dracula did not simply fly. Others explained that sunlight was dangerous to him in this story. Understanding that limit was essential: clearing a path alone would not provide the shelter he needed.
panels.artBrief: Helpful exchange among festivalgoers, sun visible overhead and Dracula remaining shaded; captions identify fantasy rule.

chapters.title: An Apology Above the Clouds
chapters.learningFocus: Identify the parts of an accountable apology and distinguish apology from automatic forgiveness.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: Dracula reached Jonathan’s aeroplane after it had taken off. In bat form, he flew beside the window and tried to get the traveller’s attention. He had left the shaded help of the crowd, and sunlight now made the effort painful.
panels.artBrief: Clearly fantastical bat flight beside aircraft window, small smoke wisps only, no realistic aircraft access instructions.

panels.narration: Jonathan recognised the talking bat, but the noise and glass made communication difficult. Dracula tried to say he was sorry. The words were misunderstood, turning an important apology into a confused exchange across the window.
panels.artBrief: Split view inside and outside aircraft, sound separation evident; adapted text avoids copying source joke verbatim.

panels.narration: Jonathan noticed the sunlight affecting him. Dracula could not keep trying forever, so he found another way to speak. His magical solution belonged to the fantasy world of the story, not to ordinary travel or communication.
panels.artBrief: Jonathan concerned at window; bat strained, no burns or injury details; fantasy glow signals impossible method.

panels.narration: Using magic, Dracula spoke through the pilot’s announcement. This time Jonathan could hear him clearly. The count admitted that he had made a terrible mistake and began explaining it without blaming his daughter for wanting a different life.
panels.artBrief: Aircraft cabin listening to announcement, pilot visible only as neutral distant silhouette; no cockpit operational details.

panels.narration: He accepted responsibility for trying to keep Mavis to himself. Protecting her had become an excuse to stop her discovering things. He now recognised that growing up includes difficult experiences as well as happiness, and that he could not choose them all for her.
panels.artBrief: Honest announcement heard by Johnny; symbolic memory images of closed door and daughter’s hopes, clearly recalled not new events.

panels.narration: Dracula said he valued the connection between Mavis and Jonathan. Rather than ordering the human away, he was thankful that his daughter trusted him. The apology included a changed understanding, not only the word “sorry.”

dialogue.speaker: Dracula, through the announcement
dialogue.text: I am thankful that she trusts you.

panels.artBrief: Close-up of Jonathan listening, expression softens; current physical location remains aircraft.

panels.narration: He asked for forgiveness. Jonathan saw him outside and answered with a smile and a thumbs-up. The response belonged to Jonathan: Dracula could ask honestly, but he could not command someone else to forgive him.
panels.artBrief: Window two-shot of smiling Johnny giving clear thumbs-up and relieved bat outside; correct hand anatomy.

panels.narration: Through the same fantasy magic, the aircraft turned back. The passengers were not pleased by the interruption, but Dracula’s purpose had changed. He was no longer trying to prevent a meeting; he was trying to make a reunion possible.
panels.artBrief: Distant plane turning in sky, bat maintaining flight; no specific aviation procedure, final hopeful composition.

comprehension.prompt: How did Dracula finally make his apology understandable to Jonathan?
comprehension.answerGuidance: He used magic to speak through the pilot’s announcement so Jonathan could hear him inside the aircraft.
comprehension.hint: Contrast the failed window conversation with the method that works.

comprehension.prompt: Which part of Dracula’s apology seems most important to you, and why? Use a specific detail.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept choosing his admission, responsibility, changed understanding, appreciation of Jonathan or request for forgiveness. Require explanation rather than a single preferred component.
comprehension.hint: What shows a change beyond simply saying “sorry”?

comprehension.prompt: Why should an apology not demand that the other person forgive immediately? Explain your view.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a reason about the other person’s feelings, choice or time needed to rebuild trust. No disclosure of personal conflict is required.
comprehension.hint: Think about what the person apologising can control and what they cannot.

comprehension.prompt: What three details show that Dracula’s attitude towards Mavis and Jonathan has changed?
comprehension.answerGuidance: He admits trying to keep her to himself, recognises her need to discover life, values their connection, thanks Jonathan for being trusted and asks forgiveness rather than ordering him away. Require three.
comprehension.hint: Look for different kinds of change: responsibility, belief and action.

comprehension.prompt: How do the split inside-and-outside views help explain the failed conversation at the window?
comprehension.answerGuidance: They show physical separation, noise and the barrier of glass, helping the reader understand why lip-reading or shouted words fail and a new channel is needed.
comprehension.hint: What obstacle can you see that the dialogue alone might not explain?

chapters.title: A Backpack and a New Beginning
chapters.learningFocus: Assess sincerity using both words and actions; explain how independence can coexist with care.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: Dracula returned to the hotel tired and affected by the sun, but determined to speak honestly. He told Mavis that he had thought the worst thing would be watching her leave. Now he understood that seeing her unhappy was worse.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: I want you to live your life.

panels.artBrief: Father tired with lightly singed cape edge, no burns, daughter concerned; quiet reunion in familiar room.

panels.narration: Mavis did not immediately know how to begin again. Her father’s changed words mattered, but the hurt had not disappeared. A sincere apology needed to be followed by an action she could understand.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: I do not know how to do that now.

panels.artBrief: Mavis hesitant, father patient, no instant happy reaction before surprise.

panels.narration: Dracula offered a birthday present of his own: a black-and-pink backpack. It was a different kind of gift from the protected hotel. A bag could suggest movement, choices and experiences beyond the place where she had always lived.

dialogue.speaker: Mavis
dialogue.text: What do I need this for?

panels.artBrief: Backpack held front-facing, colour consistent with source, no commercial logo required; Jonathan hidden from viewer at first.

panels.narration: He turned it to reveal an unexpected companion: Jonathan had returned. Mavis was surprised, then asked why he was there after his cruel goodbye. The reunion could not be honest unless they addressed the words that had hurt her.
panels.artBrief: Reveal composition showing Johnny behind the presented bag, no impossible person inside tiny bag; warm surprise.

panels.narration: Jonathan said that their connection mattered to him. He admitted that fear of Dracula’s threat had influenced what he said before leaving. His earlier rejection had not been a truthful account of his feelings for Mavis.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.text: I was afraid of your father.

panels.artBrief: Jonathan explains with remorse, Mavis attentive; father visible and listening, no threatening flashback illustration.

panels.narration: Dracula did not keep denying his part. He admitted that he had been wrong. This allowed them to begin to reconcile, although the story did not need to pretend that a single sentence could erase every hurt instantly.
panels.artBrief: Three-person honest exchange, father shoulders lowered rather than commanding, no forced embrace.

panels.narration: He encouraged Mavis to make a life of her own. Her independence did not mean he had stopped caring about her. It meant he was beginning to support her choices instead of using fear to prevent them.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: Go and make your own paradise.

panels.artBrief: Father steps aside from doorway instead of blocking it, symbolic visual echo of chapter1; Mavis and Johnny together.

panels.narration: When Mavis and Jonathan moved closer again, Dracula briefly reacted with his old alarm. Then he caught himself and admitted he needed practice. Change had begun, but he was still learning how to be a caring father without holding every choice in his hands.

dialogue.speaker: Dracula
dialogue.text: I am still getting used to this.

panels.artBrief: Brief comic startled face followed by sheepish smile; age-appropriate affection, no final new travel departure invented.

comprehension.prompt: How can someone become more independent while still staying connected to people who care about them?
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept a practical balance of choices, communication and appropriate support. No private family disclosure is required.
comprehension.hint: Independence does not have to mean doing everything alone.

chapters.title: A Different Kind of Happy Ending
chapters.learningFocus: Review the full story, explain a theme with evidence and compare the ending with the beginning.
chapters.adaptationLabel: Original Grade 5 adaptation of the user-supplied transcript; narration and speech are adapted, not verbatim film quotations.

panels.narration: Music returned to the hotel. Jonathan led a lively performance, and the guests joined the celebration. The painful interruption did not become the only memory of Mavis’s birthday; the characters now had a chance to end it together.
panels.artBrief: Full ballroom finale with familiar band and guests, warm rich colour, no film song lyrics embedded in illustration.

panels.narration: The song celebrated what the characters called a “zing,” their story’s name for a special connection. Mavis and the others joined in. The scene showed affection and energy rather than a new argument about who belonged at the hotel.
panels.artBrief: Mavis, Murray and Johnny perform together, Dracula nearby listening, no new plot or sequel characters.

panels.narration: Jonathan invited Dracula to perform. At first, the father claimed he had only moved closer to listen. Then he agreed to try. Joining the music was a small action, but it contrasted with his earlier insistence on controlling every part of the party.
panels.artBrief: Dracula at edge of stage, initial hesitation followed by willing step forward.

panels.narration: Soon Dracula was performing with the group. Their cooperation created an ending nobody could have produced alone. The hidden hotel had become a place where a human visitor and monsters could celebrate together, at least among the people shown in this story.
panels.artBrief: Finale performance, father joins rather than replacing others; joyful inclusive ensemble, no claim hotel policies legally or permanently changed.

panels.narration: LOOKING BACK: At the beginning, Dracula shut a door when Mavis asked about the world. Later, he encouraged her independence. The contrast showed that caring for someone could change from preventing every risk to supporting their own discoveries.
panels.artBrief: Clearly labelled recap panel: left closed door from chapter1, right father stepping aside from chapter23. These are memories, not new events.

panels.narration: LOOKING BACK: Disguises and invented explanations had created confusion. Honest admissions began the repair. Forgiveness did not make the earlier choices harmless; it gave the characters a way to move forward while recognising what had happened.
panels.artBrief: Recap strip of slipped disguise, honest apology and reunion, labelled as earlier moments; no new act of forgiveness invented.

panels.narration: LOOKING BACK: The festival crowd had helped someone the monsters expected to fear. That experience challenged an unfair judgement. The story offered evidence of kindness and cooperation without needing to claim that every person everywhere would behave identically.
panels.artBrief: Recap of cape tunnel from chapter21 in a framed memory vignette with consistent cast and costumes.

panels.narration: The final image returned to the music and the people sharing it. Mavis had not yet completed every journey she imagined, and Dracula was still learning. The hopeful ending came from a changed direction: more honesty, more trust and room for discovery.
panels.artBrief: Return to current finale, panoramic full cast joyful together; do not invent an actual Hawaii trip, marriage, sequel or future outcome.

comprehension.prompt: Who invited Dracula to join the final performance?
comprehension.answerGuidance: Jonathan invited him to perform.
comprehension.hint: Find the invitation rather than everyone who later sings.

comprehension.prompt: Does this feel like a satisfying ending? Explain using one improvement and one issue the characters may still need to work on.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept any supported judgement. Improvements include reconciliation, honesty, shared celebration or support for independence; ongoing work includes trust and Dracula’s habits. Do not require a perfect ending.
comprehension.hint: A satisfying ending can leave room for continued growth.

comprehension.prompt: What is one lesson from a story that could help someone handle a disagreement differently? Explain a hypothetical example.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Accept an applicable lesson and a clear example. A personal disclosure is not required, and no single moral is mandatory.
comprehension.hint: Choose a practical action, such as checking an assumption or admitting a mistake.

comprehension.prompt: Compare Dracula near the beginning and near the end of the story. Explain two changes using specific scenes.
comprehension.answerGuidance: Possible contrasts: closes a door versus supports independence; claims all humans are dangerous versus accepts help; lies versus acknowledges mistakes; controls entertainment versus joins it. Require two comparisons with scenes.
comprehension.hint: Use the clearly marked recap panels, or name earlier chapters you remember.

comprehension.prompt: Why are panels 5–7 labelled “LOOKING BACK” instead of being presented as new events?
comprehension.answerGuidance: The labels signal a retrospective summary and distinguish earlier evidence from the current celebration, avoiding a false impression that events are repeating or happening after the ending.
comprehension.hint: What confusion could arise without those time labels?
